text: Every finance lesson in this chapter has included a caveat. This lesson collects those caveats into one place, states them without hedging, and gives you a clear framework for evaluating any future claim you encounter about quantum computing for finance.

Pulling together what's already been said explicitly: the 3-asset portfolio QUBO was a faithful formulation exercise, but current hardware hasn't demonstrated an advantage over classical solvers at real portfolio scale. Amplitude estimation's quadratic speedup is mathematically proven, but realizing it in wall-clock terms needs fault-tolerant hardware that doesn't exist yet. And QAOA and VQE generally are heuristics without a guarantee of finding the true optimum, facing barren plateaus that worsen with scale, neither shown to outperform strong classical methods on any industrially-sized problem.

Here is the single most important distinction in the entire course. A mathematical proof that an algorithm has better asymptotic scaling is not the same claim as 'this algorithm currently runs faster or better than the best classical alternative on real problems.' Amplitude estimation's scaling is a proven theorem. Whether a quantum computer today actually delivers a faster real-world calculation is a separate, empirical question -- and as of today, across essentially every application examined in this chapter, the honest answer is 'not yet demonstrated at practically relevant scale.'

When you encounter a claim about quantum computing solving a finance problem, ask four questions in order. Is the claimed speedup theoretical, or an empirical wall-clock comparison against a strong baseline? What problem size was actually tested -- realistic, or toy scale? Was the comparison against the best available classical method? And does the claim distinguish 'ran on a simulator' from 'ran on real noisy hardware'? A claim that survives all four honestly is rare and worth taking seriously; most marketing-driven claims fail at least one, usually silently.

Next lesson's lab puts the full formulate-then-solve pipeline to work on a new 4-asset portfolio problem -- one with a counterintuitive result that should make you second-guess any 'just pick the highest-return assets' intuition.
